name: Turbinate reduction

lead: Turbinates are folds of tissue inside the nose that warm and humidify air. When the inferior turbinates are enlarged they block airflow, and turbinate reduction shrinks them. People look at it as a companion to septoplasty or rhinoplasty, so the nose breathes well as well as being reshaped.

The chain runs from smaller turbinates to clearer nasal breathing to a functional base for nose reshaping. It is a breathing operation rather than a cosmetic one. A review counted at least 13 techniques used over 130 years, and a randomised trial of 382 patients compared six techniques over six years of follow-up.

paras: It is usually done as part of a wider nasal operation, often alongside septoplasty or rhinoplasty. Techniques include removing tissue, cautery by electric, laser or radiofrequency methods, cryotherapy, and submucosal resection, with or without moving the bone outward. In looksmaxxing forums it comes up in breathing-focused threads next to jaw and palate expansion.

Reviews describe a lack of well-designed comparative studies, and the aim in the literature is to reduce symptoms while preserving turbinate function. Forum posters cite empty nose syndrome after aggressive reduction as a concern; its status is debated among clinicians. It is performed by surgeons and carries the general risks of nasal surgery.

angle.text: People pair turbinate reduction with septoplasty or rhinoplasty so the nose breathes well and can be reshaped on a functional base. Smaller turbinates clear the airway, which is the point of the operation rather than a cosmetic change. Studies cover airway outcomes, and forum posters discuss trade-offs such as empty nose syndrome.

lead: Turbinate reduction is a group of surgical procedures that reduce the size of the inferior turbinates, the mucosa-covered structures on the side walls of the nasal cavity, to relieve nasal obstruction. It is often combined with septoplasty or rhinoplasty because enlargement can occur on the side opposite a deviated septum, described as compensatory hypertrophy.[1][1]

A review of techniques counted at least 13 methods over 130 years and reported a serious lack of qualified studies, with prospective randomised comparisons being extremely rare. Its authors stated that the purpose of surgery should be to reduce complaints while preserving turbinate function.[2] A later randomised trial of 382 patients compared six techniques over six years of follow-up.[3]
In looksmaxxing communities the procedure is discussed mostly as a breathing intervention and compared with maxillary expansion, with some members warning against aggressive reduction.[4]
infobox: Turbinectomy, cautery (electro, laser, radiofrequency), cryotherapy, submucosal resection

paras: Turbinate hypertrophy can contribute to persistent nasal obstruction, and a paper on nasal airway obstruction describes turbinates among its anatomic contributors.[5] Turbinates warm and humidify inspired air, and a review of the controversies notes that obstruction can persist after septorhinoplasty if turbinate hypertrophy is not addressed. Allergic rhinitis, a common cause of turbinate swelling, is the subject of a clinical practice guideline.[6]

The Siena randomised trial grouped patients into turbinectomy, laser cautery, electrocautery, cryotherapy, submucosal resection, and submucosal resection with lateral displacement.[3] Other reports describe alternative reduction techniques considered safe by their authors.[7] Registered trials have compared partial resection with radiofrequency ablation, and studied reduction under local anaesthesia.[8][9]

Randomised studies from the 1990s examined compensatory inferior turbinate hypertrophy after septoplasty and evaluated turbinoplasty with acoustic rhinometry and long-term follow-up.[1][10] A study of the NOSE scale in septoplasty without turbinate reduction compared the scale with other measures.[11] Registered trials are examining septoplasty with and without turbinate reduction.[12][13]

Reviews emphasise preserving turbinate function when reducing tissue.[2] On looksmax.org, one poster told others to look up empty nose syndrome and avoid reduction, while another replied that reduction is the only fix for true turbinate obstruction.[4] The sources reviewed here do not contain a study of empty nose syndrome.
Opioid use after rhinoplasty has also been studied as part of peri-operative care.[14]

A 382-patient randomised trial compared six reduction techniques over six years.[3] Randomised studies examined turbinoplasty after septoplasty.[1][10] The review literature judges comparative evidence to be scarce.[2] Registered trials include a terminated phase 4 study of surgical reduction for obstruction, a completed trial of radiofrequency reduction in persistent allergic rhinitis, a 242-patient trial of turbinate reduction to improve CPAP outcomes in sleep apnoea, and a trial of reduction under local anaesthesia.[15][16][17][9]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org turbinate reduction is mentioned in nasal-breathing threads, often compared with maxillary expansion.[4]

claims.claim: Turbinate reduction should be avoided at all costs because of empty nose syndrome.
If turbinates are truly oversized, reduction is the only thing that fixes the blockage.
